Winter in Shanghai, the Magic City

Last year it was all gloom and rain

This year the word is definitely sunshine

Another bright and sunny weekend

I wake up

Jay Chou’s finally dropped a new song

And me?

Still no idea what to write for the next post

That deadline’s lurking, eyeing me up

What to do?

Fire up QQ Music, put on my blue QC35s

Off to the pool

Breaststroke, freestyle, fifteen hundred to start

Yo~ Yo~

#I believe so deeply#

#that it’s you standing behind me#

~~~

#Two hands play out the dawn#

#So this is how sweet love can sound#

~~~

After 1,500 meters of splashing, I step into the shower stall, and mingling with the hiss of the water is Jay Chou’s new song. No idea who was singing, but not bad at all!

Jay Chou is still Jay Chou. (For readers outside the Chinese-speaking world: Jay Chou is the Taiwanese superstar of Mandarin pop, and “Aiyo, not bad!” is his famous catchphrase.)

The moment Er Mu turned on the shower, the topic for this post seemed to arrive.

Technology makes life more convenient, but it also makes it ever faster. After a busy day of work or study, you come home at night more or less exhausted. Apart from belly-flopping onto the bed like a gymnast and lying there like a salted fish for a while,

another great way to shake off the fatigue may be to go and take a shower.

As the temperature rises, white steam slowly fills the room and your view gradually blurs. Right now you feel as if you are standing center stage at a stadium concert, with white dry-ice fog rising around you in front of ten thousand fans.

Without thinking, you raise your right hand, pick up the microphone that is yours and yours alone, clear your throat and begin your performance.

When you get to the chorus you love, you sometimes even pause to savor the voice you just heard, which seems lovely enough to linger in the air for a while. (Narrator: Hmm, I must sound so good that even God can’t bear to let the notes vanish right away.)

I bet plenty of people have had an experience like this in the shower. Those of you who aren’t very confident about your singing and stay shy and reserved at karaoke will belt it out in the shower, just like the guy and the girl in these GIFs. Do you recognize yourselves in them?

Many people like singing in the shower because they feel they sound better there than anywhere else.

So what causes that feeling?

Is it that the small space and the relaxed setting

temporarily improve our singing?

Or is it just an illusion?

The answer actually has nothing to do with us. It lies in the bathroom where we shower, usually tiled on every side. The bathroom edits and dresses up our voice in three ways: loudness, reverberation and bass boost.

Loudness

Bathroom floors and walls are usually covered in waterproof tiles. To sound waves, a tiled surface is almost perfectly rigid: when sound reaches the wall, almost none of it is absorbed. It is reflected straight back, hits another wall, is reflected back again, and so on, bouncing around the little space until the air has absorbed it completely. These reflections make the sound more intense (louder), so our voices sound more powerful.

Reverberation

The rigid walls fill the room with reflections. These reflections travel paths of different lengths to reach our ears, and since the speed of sound is fixed, they arrive at different times. That is why we seem to keep hearing a sound for a little while after it is made (no, God has nothing to do with it). This is called reverberation, formally defined as the persistence of sound in a room after the source has stopped. Reverberation makes our voices sound richer and fuller, rather than as “dry” as in an ordinary room.

Another benefit of reverberation is that it helps with intonation: even if you are a little off-key, it still sounds perfectly fine. In fact, many karaoke systems add digital reverb (Er Mu may have stumbled on the truth here ).

The same kind of reverberation is common in stairwells and underground car parks. For a while, videos of strangers chiming in to finish each other’s songs in such places were all the rage on Douyin (the Chinese version of TikTok). The video below may be the one that started the trend. Enjoy the lovely singing, or the touching story, and listen to the reverberation while you’re at it.

#Deep in the forest, you see the deer#

#An old tree keeps the old house company#

Bass boost

A bathroom is usually a rectangular box, and the tiled walls give it acoustically rigid boundaries. Basic acoustic theory says such a room has many normal-mode (resonance) frequencies, and sound at those frequencies is amplified to a greater or lesser extent. In a bathroom of ordinary size, the fundamental mode is around 100 Hz, and many of its multiples are also modal frequencies (the density of modes increases with frequency). These frequencies happen to fall in the lower half of the speech band (80–10,000 Hz). Amplifying the lower modal frequencies makes our voices sound a bit fuller and deeper.

In short, we sound better singing in the shower mainly because the bathroom works as a million-yuan mixing engineer. Er… well, a hundred-thousand-yuan one at least…

Because they sound better than usual, many people start singing in the shower without even thinking about it. Singing in the shower has another benefit too: it helps you shake off fatigue.

For one thing, singing makes us breathe deeply, getting more oxygen into the blood and speeding up the metabolism.

For another, deep breathing works a bit like meditation and helps us relax.

And finally, while we’re lost in our own singing, all our worries disappear, at least for that moment.

So singing your heart out in the shower really is a great option!

EVERYBODY!

PUT YOUR HANDS UP!

PUT YOUR HANDS UP!

Everyone’s a rock star in the bathroom!!!
